title: Views
html:
A view is a saved query that behaves like a table. It stores no data (unless materialised) — every time you select from it, its query runs.

Creating and using a view

Simplicity

Hide complex joins behind a simple name; analysts query employee_directory, not four joins.

Security

Grant access to a view that exposes some columns/rows (no salary) instead of the base table.

Stable interface

Refactor the underlying tables while the view keeps the old shape for existing reports.

Consistency

One definition of “active customer” or “net revenue” instead of ten copies.

A view for business logic

Updatable views

A simple view over one table without aggregates, DISTINCT or GROUP BY is usually updatable in PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQL Server and Oracle. WITH CHECK OPTION rejects writes that would fall outside the view's WHERE.

SQLite

SQLite views are read-only; you make them writable with INSTEAD OF triggers (see Triggers).

Materialised views

A materialised view stores the query result physically, so reads are fast but data is only as fresh as the last refresh. Great for heavy dashboards.

ViewMaterialised view
Stores dataNo — query runs on every readYes — a snapshot
FreshnessAlways currentStale until refreshed
Read speedSame as the underlying queryFast (can be indexed)
Write costNoneRefresh cost
What is the difference between a view and a table?

A table stores rows. A (regular) view stores only a query; reading it runs the query against the base tables, so it is always up to date and uses no extra storage. Views give abstraction and security; they don't make queries faster by themselves.

Can you insert into a view?

If the view is updatable — typically a single base table, no aggregates/DISTINCT/GROUP BY/set operators, and it includes all NOT NULL columns without defaults. Otherwise, use INSTEAD OF triggers (SQL Server, Oracle, PostgreSQL, SQLite).
